title: Playing the DeLux in Chicago and joining the union
summary: His band played at the DeLux on 35th and State and was forced into the union by the owner after union pressure.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: I traveled all around. Yeah. And then I come back, you know, and I got a job. Well, we went over in Chicago, such as Blue Monday, Blue Wednesday, Blue Tuesday, the Dreamland and have it on Mondays. DeLux would have it on Tuesdays, T9 Jones, number two, like, different days. And all the entertainers would go from one place to another. So we went on, they invited us to come over to the DeLux. I was upstairs over to Old Panama's, right Old Panama Club. It's been 35th and State. I went up there and playing, everybody was crazy about it. In the Orleans Jazz Band, I was during that time slapping bass, all the hornets around me like that, you know. Yeah.

Yeah, so. So Shaw said, how would you like to work up there? How would you like your band up there? I said, all right. He said, all right, I'll give you a job. I said, okay. Well, it didn't belong to the Union. Well, we played there a couple of weeks, you know. Finally, the cards kept coming there. Well, they had three men playing there. They played for the entertainers. Cora, Cora, Caroline Williams, Florence Mills, Brick Top, Cora Williams, and another girl, Justine, this Justine girl. They played for the entertainers. These three fellas, clarinet, piano, and drums. They came out and said, you fellas belong to the Union, I'll have to get the Union. I said, who? I'll get no Union. I know it's get the Union, you're going to freeze me out. That's what you know. I'll have to do Union. I said, no, no, nobody can freeze you out. You got your band to freeze you out for what? I said, oh, no. I said, oh, I'm telling you, you got John's Union. Everybody's Union here and you all can't play here. Finally, old Copeland come down, the secretary, one day. I said, who's the leader? All that girls. They said, you boys will have to come on in, take out a card. I said, well, take out a card for what? Well, I want to be in Union. I got my own group. He said, that's all right, but you're working in the Union house. And everything was Union. Waiters in the hall was Union in there. Oh, I couldn't see it. He said, well, all right. He said, if you boys don't join the Union, he told Mr. Shaw, he says, we'll have to pull these other boys out of here and we're going to pull these waiters. So Mr. Shaw comes to me and he said, that night, he said, you done have me to check out. Give me a check. Just take this down to Union and take your boys down. I said, I don't join them. They're going to mess it. They ain't going to mess up. You're working here for me. They say, you got the Johnny Union. Just take that and just go on down there. That's how I got in the Union. Shaw gave me the check and made the band join the Union. And we joined the Union. And them guys used to hang around with Sugar Johnny, you know, poor sugar. He had Sugar Johnny blow, you know. And then I stayed there quite a while. And then this fellow Nick Williams, George Williams, opened up the club on 34th Street. It was called, what do you call that club? He named the tune after it.
It was called the Royal Garden.
